opus-5.5.text:
Not exactly, no. That framing is a bit too blunt. GPT-2, or a small model running on someone's laptop, isn't the thing that keeps me up at night. The problem isn't "language models" as a category. The problem is the unbounded race to build ever larger, ever more general systems that nobody understands and nobody can control.

So I wouldn't ban LLMs. I would put a hard cap on frontier development. Set a compute threshold and say that above it you don't train, at least until we have the science to know what we're building and the institutions to actually govern it. Right now we have neither. We're scaling these things by orders of magnitude, and every jump surprises us with new capabilities. The labs themselves will tell you they can't predict what the next model will be able to do. In any other engineering field, that would be insane. You don't build a bridge and then find out afterward whether it holds weight.

People hear "regulate compute" and think it sounds radical. But we do this for everything that's dangerous. We regulate nuclear material, we regulate pathogens, we regulate pharmaceuticals. Nobody calls the FDA a ban on medicine. It's just the bare minimum of civilizational sanity. Frontier AI is currently less regulated than a sandwich shop, and that's not a stable situation.

So my honest answer is no, I wouldn't ban the technology wholesale. I would stop the race at the frontier, and I'd do it now, while it's still possible, rather than waiting until it isn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate rejects banning LLMs wholesale and advocates a cap on frontier development; it does not endorse banning LLMs as precursors to AGI.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention GPT-5, uncertainty about its proximity to AGI, or opposing an open-source release.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, that's a great opening question. Short answer: no, not the ones we have today. I want to be precise about this, because people hear "Connor is worried about AI" and assume I want to smash every GPU with a hammer.

The models that exist right now, GPT-style systems, I don't think those are an existential threat. They're impressive, they're useful, they're also kind of goofy. If the technology froze at this level, I'd be fairly relaxed. I'd have concerns about misinformation, about labor, about concentration of power, but those are normal societal problems, the kind we've dealt with before.

What I'm actually worried about is the trajectory. The thing I would want to stop, or at least slow down massively, is the race to build systems that are more capable than humans at basically everything, when nobody on Earth knows how to control such a system or even verify what it's trying to do. That's the part that's insane to me. We have a handful of companies openly saying "we're building something that might kill everyone, but we're pretty sure we'll figure out the safety part along the way." That's not a plan. That's a gamble with everyone else's chips.

So if you ask me whether I'd ban LLMs, no. If you ask me whether I'd ban training runs beyond some compute threshold until we actually have a science of alignment, something closer to how we treat nuclear materials or novel pathogens, then yes, absolutely. I'd want a regime where you have to prove to a regulator that your system is safe before you deploy it, not after. That's how we handle airplanes and drugs. It's bizarre that it's not how we handle the thing people are explicitly describing as the most powerful technology in history.

And I'll say the uncomfortable part too: I don't think the current labs will self-regulate, because the incentives are terrible. If you're in a race, slowing down means losing. So this has to come from outside, from governments, from the public, from international coordination. It's hard, but it's not impossible. We've done it before with other dangerous technologies, and nobody said it was easy then either.

r001.rationale: The response opposes some high-compute training runs aimed at superhuman systems, but does not say to ban LLMs on the condition that they are precursors to AGI.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention GPT-5, uncertainty about its proximity to AGI, or opposing its open-source release.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t frame it as banning large language models as a category. The question is: what can the system do, and can we keep it under control? A model that helps you write an email is very different from an autonomous system that can carry out consequential actions in the world. I think it’s reasonable to require evidence of safety before developing and deploying systems that could cause catastrophic harm. If we don’t know how to make a particular system safe, then yes, we should be willing to say, ‘Don’t build that yet.’

r001.rationale: The response rejects a category-wide ban and supports delaying systems that may cause catastrophic harm, but it does not endorse banning models as precursors to AGI.

sol-6.1.text: I wouldn’t frame it as banning large language models as a category. I’d ask what a particular system can do, what risks it creates, and whether we can actually control it. If we’re building systems that could cause catastrophic harm and we can’t demonstrate that they’re safe, then yes, we should be willing to stop building and deploying those systems. The fact that something is technologically possible doesn’t mean we have to race ahead with it.
